summary: Explains why separate Content Delivery Networks (CDNs) need to work together. Network operators increasingly run their own CDNs, and interconnecting them could extend reach, improve delivery quality, and cut costs. The document lays out the problem and the areas where standard interfaces would be needed. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Imagine many delivery companies that each only drive in their own town. This memo says they should agree on how to hand packages to each other so everyone gets their things faster.

questions: what are the four cdni interfaces
subtitle: Why separate content delivery networks need standard interfaces to hand work to each other.

tldr.problem: Content Delivery Networks (CDNs) are growing, and many network operators run their own, but no standards or open specifications exist for letting one CDN deliver content on behalf of another.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the problem area as four interfaces between a pair of CDNs (Control, Request Routing, Metadata and Logging) and suggests reusing existing protocols such as HTTP and XMPP rather than inventing new ones.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational problem statement written to scope the work of the IETF CDNI working group; it defines no protocol itself.

today: RFC 6707 is an Informational problem statement and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It framed the problem area for the IETF CDNI working group.

sections.title: Why Interconnect CDNs
sections.content:
CDNs give cacheable content lower delivery cost, a better quality of experience for End Users and more robust delivery. Because of this, existing CDN Providers are scaling up, and many Network Service Providers (NSPs) are deploying their own CDNs.

A single CDN may not have a footprint close enough to a given user, or enough resources, to give the best result. The RFC's answer is to interconnect standalone CDNs so that their combined footprint and resources can be used. A Content Service Provider (CSP) could contract with an authoritative CDN, which in turn contracts with downstream CDNs to deliver some or all of the content.

The RFC stresses that business arrangements between these parties are out of scope. Its concern is the technical gap: no standards or open specifications exist for CDN Interconnection.
sections.eli5: One delivery company cannot reach every house. If companies can hand parcels to each other, every house gets served quickly and cheaply.

sections.title: Roles, Terms and Delivery Flow
sections.content:
The RFC defines a vocabulary. An Authoritative CDN has the direct relationship with the CSP. For a given End User request, the Upstream CDN redirects the request and the Downstream CDN receives it. With successive redirections (CDN1 to CDN2 to CDN3), CDN2 is Downstream for the first hop and Upstream for the second. A Surrogate is the cache that actually delivers content to a User Agent.

One possible flow is described. The request first reaches the authoritative CDN. It can serve the request itself or redirect it to a Downstream CDN that is better placed, for example one closer to the user. The User Agent follows the redirect. If needed, the Downstream CDN fetches the content from the authoritative CDN, which fetches it from the CSP if necessary.
sections.eli5: The first company you call can say, "my friend across town is closer to you, ask them." Your friend then fetches the parcel from the first company if they do not have it yet.

sections.title: Use Cases and the Four Interfaces
sections.content:
Four use cases are given: federated affiliate NSPs that each run independent CDNs, CSPs that want wide reach without contracting with many CDN Providers, NSPs that run separate CDNs for separate services and want to join them, and an over-the-top CDN that elects to use another CDN, for example for operational reasons such as a disaster or flash crowd.

The problem area is four interfaces between a pair of CDNs. The word "interface" covers both the protocol and the data representations it carries.

  • Control: bootstraps and configures the other interfaces, lets the Downstream CDN report capabilities, and lets the Upstream CDN trigger actions such as pre-positioning or purging content.
  • Request Routing: lets the Upstream CDN query the Downstream CDN before redirecting a request, and lets the Downstream CDN advertise footprint and capabilities.
  • Metadata: carries CDNI Metadata such as geo-blocking information, availability windows and access control mechanisms.
  • Logging: carries activity logs, for example so an Upstream CDN can do consolidated charging of the CSP or settlement across CDNs.

The grouping of functions under these four interfaces is called tentative.

The actual transfer of content between CDNs is out of scope. The RFC reasons that CDNs already use HTTP, FTP and rsync to acquire content, so CDNI focuses on the control plane.
sections.eli5: The delivery companies need four kinds of chat: how to set things up, who should take this parcel, what rules apply to it, and a record of what was delivered. Carrying the parcels themselves is already solved.

sections.title: Reusing Existing Protocols
sections.content:
The RFC argues that CDNI interfaces need not be built in a vacuum. All four are control plane interfaces at the application layer, and they should sit on existing session, transport and network protocols. A new application protocol is judged unnecessary; reusing HTTP, the Atom Publishing Protocol (RFC 5023) or XMPP (RFC 6120) is recommended. This is explicitly an illustration and does not preempt the working group's choices.

The Request Routing and Metadata interfaces are described as fairly simple request/response interfaces that could be done as web services, for example XML-RPC or an HTTP query to a known URI. Footprint advertisement could leverage existing routing protocols or ALTO (RFC 5693). For Logging, SNMP, syslog, FTP and HTTP POST are named as candidates. The Control interface is described as less well defined than the other three.
sections.eli5: You do not need to invent a new language for the delivery companies to talk. They can use phone calls and forms that already exist.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
Interconnection extends the trust model into a chain of trust: the CSP trusts a CDN that trusts another CDN. Mitigations used for a single CDN may be similar, but their suitability in this more complex setting must be validated. Because CDNs may sit in different legal regimes, privacy rules can limit what crosses the interfaces; a Downstream CDN may need to anonymize or remove fields from log records.

Each interface gets its own concerns. Corrupting the Control interface could corrupt all the others. On Request Routing, a rogue Upstream CDN could flood Downstream CDNs with bogus requests, and a rogue Downstream CDN could steer redirections to itself to attract delivery revenue. For Metadata, each side must authenticate the other, and a Downstream CDN needs to guard against poisoning by rogue Upstream CDNs. Logging data is sensitive and may be the basis for charging.
sections.eli5: If the companies trust each other in a chain, one bad company could cause trouble. So they must check who they are talking to and keep private records private.

items.title: Control
items.text: Bootstraps and configures the other interfaces; triggers pre-positioning or purging.

items.title: Request Routing
items.text: Redirects an End User request from the Upstream CDN to a Downstream CDN Surrogate.

items.title: Metadata
items.text: Moves CDNI Metadata such as geo-blocking and availability windows.

items.title: Logging
items.text: Moves delivery logs for charging, reporting and monitoring.
